sample_members.antecedent: Sound waves propagating in porous material
sample_members.mechanism: Sound waves lose energy due to friction between air particles and the material's void walls, and through internal reflections within the material. Deeper penetration of pressure waves into the material facilitates greater interaction and energy transfer.

sample_members.antecedent: Larger pore size in sound absorbing material
sample_members.mechanism: Larger pores facilitate increased energy transfer from the vibrating air particles to the solid structure of the material, leading to more effective sound absorption.

sample_members.antecedent: Smaller pore size in sound absorbing material
sample_members.mechanism: Smaller pores reduce the energy transfer from the vibrating air particles to the solid structure, causing more sound energy to be reflected from the surface rather than absorbed.

sample_members.antecedent: Reduction in fiber diameter of fibrous sound absorbing material
sample_members.mechanism: A reduction in fiber diameter necessitates more fibers for the same volume density, which in turn increases the air flow resistance and creates a more tortuous path for sound waves, leading to greater frictional energy dissipation.

Thicker materials are more effective at absorbing low-frequency sounds (longer wavelengths) because they provide a longer path for sound waves to interact with the material and dissipate energy. Optimal absorption occurs when thickness is at least one-tenth of the incident sound wavelength.

sample_members.antecedent: Air gap thickness behind sound absorbing material
sample_members.consequent: Sound Absorption Coefficient (SAC) in mid and higher frequencies
sample_members.mechanism: A greater air gap allows sound waves to be trapped longer, leading to more energy loss and enhanced sound absorption, particularly effective in the mid and higher frequency ranges.

For a simply connected manifold, the first homotopy group π₁(M) is trivial, meaning all closed cycles are contractible to a point. Consequently, only a trivial flat U(1) bundle is possible, as all holonomies are trivial (equal to unity). This leads to a single, unique representation (up to unitary transformations).

For a non-simply connected manifold, the first homotopy group π₁(M) is non-trivial, allowing for non-contractible closed cycles. These cycles can have non-trivial holonomies for the flat U(1) bundle, leading to an infinity of inequivalent representations, each labelled by the specific holonomies.
